comparator.name: Philosophy, Politics and Economics
comparator.sourceNotes: The 135 EC major includes eight first-year courses, three research methods courses, one thematic package, two advanced courses and a thesis. This example uses the welfare-state package and illustrates advanced study in philosophy and history. The remaining 45 EC is open for electives.
components: Major Debates in Global Economic History
The Welfare State: Past and Present

routeSelection.basis: The generic target names no thematic package. Utrecht presents four equally weighted interdisciplinary packages with no general default. The cohort regulations list Challenges to the Welfare State first. Their two advanced-choice lists likewise place Topics in Philosophy and Advanced Disciplinary Course in History first. The illustration follows this published order independently of UCR fit.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Integrated philosophy, politics, economics and history for analysing political and economic institutions
Ethics, political philosophy, justice and public-policy evaluation
Democracy, political institutions, policymaking and pressures on liberal democracy
Microeconomics, macroeconomics, markets and economic-policy reasoning
Global economic history and the historical development of political and economic institutions
Welfare states, social protection, redistribution and the balance between support, responsibility and freedom
Qualitative, quantitative and critical-reasoning methods for interdisciplinary PPE research
Independent interdisciplinary research culminating in a PPE bachelor thesis
adjacent: Markets, regulators, capitalism and relations among government, institutions and business
Sustainability policy, environmental governance, biodiversity and natural-resource scarcity
International governance, conflict, rights and public accountability
questions: How should welfare, markets and public policy balance justice, freedom, responsibility and social protection?
How can political and economic institutions govern sustainability and environmental limits fairly?
How does history help explain current political and economic problems and institutional choices?

trace: Practises scholarly inquiry, academic writing, reflection and community engagement.
Introduces market incentives, supply and demand, production and aggregate output.
Examines economic growth, macroeconomic shocks, financial markets and policy in open economies.
Studies decision-making, market power, competition and market efficiency.
Analyzes public goods, externalities, taxation, redistribution, welfare provision and social insurance.
Develops regression methods for estimation, prediction and causal inference, including instrumental variables.
Uses behavioral evidence to examine how observed choices differ from standard economic models.
Introduces study design, measurement, sampling and statistical inference.
Develops propositional and predicate logic, proof and discrete mathematical reasoning.
Develops data preparation, exploratory analysis and visualization for empirical research.
Develops calculus, optimization and mathematical modeling.
Develops matrix and vector methods that support formal economic modeling.
Develops probability models, statistical inference and simulation.
Studies flood risk, freshwater allocation, adaptation, water law and justice.
Examines collective action, resource governance, institutions and climate justice.
Studies organismal diversity, its measurement and ecological roles.
Examines farming systems, biodiversity impacts and agricultural alternatives.
Develops spatial analysis, remote sensing and geospatial evidence for environmental questions.
Introduces planetary boundaries, environmental chemistry and systems reasoning.
Develops scientific methods for examining materials and environmental processes.
Explains climate processes, emissions and the impacts of climate change.
Studies energy demand, renewable generation, storage, grids and transition constraints.
Analyzes energy use and cleaner energy systems in an applied technical and economic project.
Introduces legal traditions, public law and the relationship between law and society.
Examines industrialization, social reform, ideologies, migration and imperialism in modern history.
Uses historical cases to examine gender, social roles, family and inequality.
Examines imperial institutions, legitimacy and the economic organization of empires.
Develops independent historical inquiry, primary-source criticism and evidence-based argument.
Examines the philosophical justification and legal protection of human rights.
Examines treaties, jurisdiction, international institutions and state responsibility.
Compares constitutions, public institutions, courts and constitutional rights.
Examines EU legal competences, enforcement, the internal market and regulatory issues.
Introduces moral theories, philosophical argument and questions about knowledge.
Evaluates obligations, fairness and consequences through major ethical theories.
Examines how emotions shape judgment, knowledge and decisions.
Examines agency, free will and moral responsibility.
Examines political authority, rights and rival theories of just institutions.
Compares democratic and authoritarian institutions and examines democratic backsliding.
Examines theories of international institutions, cooperation and political economy.
Studies European governance, representation, policy formation and legitimacy.
Analyzes public policymaking through a comparative regulatory case and develops policy memo writing.
Examines social structures, stratification, solidarity and inequality.
Develops qualitative research design, interviewing, observation and interpretation.
Uses environmental justice cases to examine social movements, collective action and unequal risks.
Examines civil society, social trust and how publics form and influence institutions.
Analyzes how climate claims are framed and contested across media and develops a public communication project.

alternatives.label: Ethics, Welfare and Public Policy
alternatives.labelReason: Study how societies make decisions about welfare, rights and public spending. Combine ethics, politics, economics and history, and use qualitative, quantitative and historical research methods to examine policy choices.
alternatives.concept: Study how societies make decisions about welfare, rights and public spending. Combine ethics, politics, economics and history, and use qualitative, quantitative and historical research methods to examine policy choices.
progression: Introductory economics, politics and ethical reasoning support public economics and policy analysis. Introductory statistics and modern history precede econometrics and advanced historical inquiry.

alternatives.label: Markets, Regulation and Institutions
alternatives.labelReason: Study how public institutions shape markets. Combine economics and econometrics with comparative politics, legal institutions and history to examine regulation in national and international settings.
alternatives.concept: Study how public institutions shape markets. Combine economics and econometrics with comparative politics, legal institutions and history to examine regulation in national and international settings.
progression: Research methods and mathematical methods precede advanced economic analysis. Comparative politics and legal foundations prepare for EU politics, international law, constitutional law and EU market regulation.
alternatives.distinctness: Study how public institutions shape markets. Combine economics and econometrics with comparative politics, legal institutions and history to examine regulation in national and international settings. Compared with option 1, each plan has 9 courses unique to that plan.

alternatives.label: Sustainability Policy and Environmental Governance
alternatives.concept: Study how governments and communities respond to climate change, resource constraints and biodiversity loss. Combine environmental science and data analysis with ethics, public economics and policy.
alternatives.labelReason: Study how governments and communities respond to climate change, resource constraints and biodiversity loss. Combine environmental science and data analysis with ethics, public economics and policy.
progression: The sustainability gateways and basic methods support energy, earth observation and applied design. Comparative politics precedes public policy analysis, and introductory biodiversity precedes applied study of agriculture and habitat impacts.
alternatives.distinctness: Study how governments and communities respond to climate change, resource constraints and biodiversity loss. Combine environmental science and data analysis with ethics, public economics and policy. Compared with option 1, each plan has 16 courses unique to that plan. Compared with option 2, each plan has 14 courses unique to that plan.

selection.assessment: The welfare and public policy plan draws on all four PPE disciplines. The other plans develop the separate directions of market regulation and environmental governance. Utrecht’s integrated thematic package and required interdisciplinary thesis remain distinct.

blocks: Use 45 EC for choices such as electives, a minor, study abroad or an internship. At least 15 EC must be at intermediate level.
Both develop qualitative research design and methods. UCR approaches them through sociology.
Both use research design and statistics to assess evidence. UCR introduces methods across several fields.
Utrecht’s published curriculum gives a working title. UCR develops formal logic in a separate course.
Utrecht requires a thesis that draws on two PPE disciplines. UCR offers optional independent research outside the scheduled degree.
Both build ethical reasoning. Utrecht applies it directly to questions of public policy.
Both study political authority, rights and competing ideas about just institutions.
This example shows a philosophy option. The topic can vary.
Both compare political institutions and how democracies work. UCR also studies authoritarian regimes and democratic backsliding.
Both examine how policy is made. The UCR course develops policy analysis and memo writing through a case study.
Students bring together the PPE disciplines to investigate a question from the welfare-state package.
Both use microeconomic models to study markets and decisions. The UCR course also examines behavioral departures from standard models.
Both examine aggregate economic activity and policy. UCR gives particular attention to open economies.
Both examine social insurance and redistribution. Utrecht also considers how welfare institutions balance competing values.
Utrecht studies debates in global economic history. UCR uses modern history and the history of empires to examine industrialization and economic institutions.
Both study how political institutions and ideas developed. The UCR course covers broader themes in modern history.
Utrecht studies how welfare states developed and changed. UCR history and sociology provide wider context.
This example shows a history option. Utrecht has published a provisional course title.

notes.text: Utrecht teaches philosophy, politics, economics and history through an integrated major, a thematic package and a required thesis. At UCR, students combine courses from these fields and may pursue independent research separately.

audience.programmeDescription: This English-taught bachelor uses philosophy, politics, economics and history to study how institutions work and how societies make collective decisions.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The Utrecht example shows the welfare-state package. The UCR options emphasize welfare and public policy, market regulation, or environmental governance.
